items.title: Enacting Constructive Conflicts with AI Agents to Enhance Reconsideration among Novice Interaction Designers
items.abstract: Generative AI agents are increasingly used in interaction design to facilitate ideation, often following their own internal reasoning. These interactions tend to expand the design space. Our work explores an antagonistic role for design agents, prompting designers to engage with stakeholder tension. We built an antagonistic AI agent and examined the agent’s influence in a between-subjects experiment with 45 design students across three conditions: Self Reflection (unsupported review of the design proposal), Stepwise Guidance (written prompts that walk designers through a constructive-conflict framework), and Interactive Engagement (an AI agent that enacts the constructive-conflict framework interactively by synthesizing stakeholder pushback). The latter two conditions share the framework but differ in whether it is self-enacted or agent-enacted. Results show that, compared with Self Reflection, both the Stepwise Guidance and Interactive Engagement groups reported significantly higher self-reconsideration and made more improvements to their design proposals. Compared with Stepwise Guidance, the antagonistic agent introduced more conflictual perspectives, and participants in the Engagement condition generated and discarded more ideas. These findings suggest that an interactive agent that surfaces stakeholder pushback can support concrete design revision while keeping designers engaged with divergent perspectives.

items.title: Feasibility of an AI-simulated patient encounter delivered in group and individual learning formats for first-year medical students: a two-cohort pilot study
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language model (LLM)–based simulated patients are being evaluated for problem-based learning and case-based learning in undergraduate medical education, but delivery formats are often under-specified and outcome measurement is inconsistently reported. We assessed the feasibility and acceptability of a single LLM-driven, AI-simulated patient encounter delivered in two formats—a facilitated whole-group session and a self-paced individual session—to first-year medical students (MS1), and we describe the development and provisional status of a learner-perception survey instrument. Two non-overlapping, non-randomized MS1 cohorts at one United States medical school completed the same case (Group, n = 7; Individual, n = 12) and the Behavioral Safety Language Scale–Provisional (BSLS-P) before and after the encounter. Pre-to-post change was tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank exact tests, with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction across subscale comparisons. Feasibility outcomes (recruitment, encounter completion, survey completion, technical failures, and encounter duration) and acceptability outcomes (post-encounter engagement ratings, delivery-format preference, and open-ended comments) are reported descriptively. Of 72 students invited, 19 (26%) enrolled; all completed the encounter and paired pre/post surveys (100%), with no technical failures (no encounter was terminated and no participant was excluded), although learners reported intermittent technical problems that interrupted but did not end encounters; the group session lasted approximately 35 min and individual encounters a median of 31 min (range 17–83). Pre-to-post shifts were small and imprecise; in the Group cohort, median engagement changed by + 0.33 points (Wilcoxon r = 0.13, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.90). The largest effect—a psychological-safety gain in the Individual cohort (Wilcoxon r = 0.62)—was significant before correction ( P =0.026) but not after (adjusted P =0.20). No between-cohort comparison reached significance. A single motivation item declined by one median point in both cohorts. The modal post-encounter preference was a hybrid “solo first, then group” model (7/12, 58%). On the feasibility and acceptability indicators examined, the encounter was delivered as planned in both formats and was rated favorably by learners; these data do not address educational effectiveness. Observed pre-to-post shifts are exploratory and require confirmation in an adequately powered, randomized sample. The provisional instrument is described to support that work.

items.title: From fit and innovativeness to adoption: How perceived innovation shapes software developers’ use of generative AI
items.abstract: Structured Abstract Context Despite strong organizational pressure, software developers’ adoption of generative artificial intelligence (genAI) tools remains uneven. Software development is a high-skill, knowledge-intensive activity; yet existing technology adoption frameworks offer limited insight into how functional fit and individual disposition combine to shape developers’ acceptance of genAI as a disruptive technology. Objectives This study examines the mechanisms through which task-technology fit (TTF) and personal innovativeness in IT (PI) shape software developers’ intention to use genAI. It focuses on the mediating role of perceived genAI innovation, a higher-order construct that integrates relative advantage and compatibility from innovation diffusion theory (IDT) with perceived usefulness from the technology acceptance model (TAM). Methods An integrated adoption model was developed and tested using survey data from professional software developers as early genAI adopters in 2023. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to examine the mediating role of perceived genAI innovation in the model. Results Perceived genAI innovation fully mediates the relationship between TTF and intention to use genAI. The model explains 65.7 % of the variance in intention to use, indicating strong explanatory power. Conclusion Perceived genAI innovation specifies established adoption constructs as facets of one higher-order construct and assigns them a mediating role in technology adoption research. Whereas prior models enter fit-, belief- and disposition-based constructs as parallel direct predictors, our results indicate that functional fit is associated with adoption intent through developers’ evaluation of genAI as an innovation, while individual innovativeness retains a direct association with adoption intent. This clarifies how disruptive technologies are embraced in high-skill work settings.

items.title: From human to hybrid: Reinventing dual concern theory in the age of AI transformation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizational decision processes and stakeholder relations, shifting work toward hybrid human-AI arrangements. Dual Concern Theory (DCT) is increasingly strained in these settings because it does not explicitly incorporate AI specific risks or the distinctive role of machine agents. Using a sequential two phase design, we analyzed in-depth interviews with 26 experts from multiple sectors through Glaserian Grounded Theory (GT) and then engaged the same 26 experts in a three round Delphi assessment of the resulting cross case framework. The GT analysis surfaced 15 concepts that coalesced into three higher order components (i.e., Automation Anxiety, Ethical Concerns, and Algorithmic Uncertainty) that organized participants’ accounts of stakeholder responses during AI adoption. Theoretical coding identified Algorithmic Transparency as a cross cutting condition associated with variation between defensive and cooperative conflict modes. We formalize these insights in an AI Enhanced Dual Concern framework that integrates concern for self and others with Algorithmic Transparency and organizes their combinations as a provisional configurational typology of collaborate, compete, avoid, accommodate, and compromise. The Delphi yielded stable consensus within the originating expert panel on constructs, mappings, and governance levers, including explanations, calibrated uncertainty displays, audit trails, and human override rights. The framework advances conflict theory for hybrid human-AI contexts and connects ethics to algorithmic trust and aversion. It also offers managers a diagnostic lens for supporting cooperative stakeholder engagement. Collectively, the findings provide an empirically grounded platform for theorizing and governing conflict in the age of AI transformation.

items.title: Immersive 360° Video in TVET: A Scoping Review and Future Research Agenda
items.abstract: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) requires learning environments that connect conceptual instruction with authentic occupational practice. Access to workplaces, however, may be restricted by safety, cost, logistics, operational disruption and limited equipment. Immersive 360° video can represent real professional settings and support situated observation through head-mounted displays (HMDs), mobile devices or conventional screens. This paper presents a scoping review of immersive 360° video in TVET, workplace learning and related professional education. Guided by Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR, the review searched Scopus, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink and ScienceDirect and identified 200 records. Following deduplication and screening, 49 publications representing 47 study clusters were included. The review mapped occupational and geographical contexts, evidence types, access devices, interaction, guidance, feedback, assessment, gamification, reported outcomes and limitations. Health and care professions accounted for 23 publications (46.9%), while industrial, engineering and production contexts accounted for eight (16.3%). HMDs were the primary or sole access mode in 33 publications (67.3%), and 30 (61.2%) incorporated at least moderate interaction. Twenty-six publications (53.1%) reported empirical interventions or comparisons, although comparator designs and outcome measures varied considerably. The literature frequently reported positive outcomes for presence, engagement, satisfaction, confidence and perceived authenticity. Findings for knowledge, professional performance and transfer were less consistent: several pedagogically structured interventions produced favourable results, whereas other comparisons found outcomes similar to conventional video or instruction. The reviewed literature does not support attributing educational value to immersion alone. Guidance, meaningful interaction, explanatory feedback, reflection and connection with practical activity emerged as recurrent features of interventions reporting favourable outcomes. The review also identified an uneven evidence base, with a strong concentration in health-professions education and short-term evaluations, with relatively limited evidence from apprenticeships, authentic workplaces and safety-critical operations. Future research should prioritise workplace and safety-critical contexts, delayed assessment, authentic performance and transfer, transparent reporting of instructional design, comparative device evaluation and pedagogically purposeful gamification.

items.title: Influences of psychological distress on life satisfaction in the saudi energy sector: a comparative analysis of remote and non-remote workplace
items.abstract: Workforce planning in Saudi Arabia’s energy sector has traditionally focused on operations and safety, while employees’ psychological well-being and life satisfaction received far less attention. This gap is addressed in this study through the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) framework. The research examined how stress, anxiety, and depression influence life satisfaction among Saudi energy employees, and whether remote and non-remote employees differ on each of these four outcomes. The research design was cross-sectional and quantitative. Distress was captured with the DASS-21 and life satisfaction with the seven-point SWLS. The results showed that all three distress dimensions correlated negatively with life satisfaction. In the simultaneous regression, only depression remained a significant unique predictor (β = −0.456, p < .001). The results showed no significant differences between remote and non-remote employees in stress, anxiety, depression, or life satisfaction. Effect sizes were small and the directions were consistent (remote employees reported slightly less stress and slightly lower life satisfaction), suggesting the differences should not be treated as completely absent but cannot be confirmed in this sample. The findings provide sector-specific evidence for human-capital workforce planning under Saudi Vision 2030.

items.title: Investigating Context in How Clinicians Make Sense of AI: Qualitative Interview Study
items.abstract: Background AI-driven clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) are increasingly being introduced to enhance clinical decision-making, yet their adoption in health care remains limited. Research has examined technical, organizational, and contextual barriers to adoption, but less attention has been paid to how knowledge, values, and responsibility around AI-CDSS are constructed and negotiated in practice. Objective This study examines how clinicians and AI experts make sense of AI-CDSS by reanalyzing qualitative interview data through a feminist and constructivist science and technology studies (STS) perspective. Whereas the original study examined informational needs, this reanalysis asks how participants construct relevant knowledge, evaluate the value of AI-CDSS, and negotiate appropriate use and responsibility in clinical practice. Methods The authors conducted a reanalysis of semistructured interviews held in 2024 with clinicians (n=8) and AI experts (n=8) in the Netherlands. The original study focused on informational needs for AI-CDSS. For this analysis, a deductive coding framework based on European Commission guidelines for trustworthy AI was first applied, and the material was then inductively reorganized into 5 empirical themes. Subsequently, feminist and constructivist STS concepts were used as sensitizing concepts in an abductive analysis, and these concepts were brought into dialogue with the empirical themes to examine the sociotechnical relations underlying participants’ accounts. Results Situated knowledge shows that the informational needs of clinicians are not universal but relate to their roles and specific clinical contexts, with understanding oriented less toward technical transparency than toward actionable guidance, relevance, and integration into decision-making. Standpoint theory illuminates differences between stakeholder priorities: clinicians emphasize information on how to use and act on AI outputs within existing workflows, whereas AI experts focus more on providing technical characteristics and performance metrics. Tinkering captures how clinicians experiment with AI systems in practice to develop situated, lay forms of expertise. Situated value highlights that perceptions of an AI-CDSS’s worth are relational, with clinicians valuing novel, context-sensitive insights and developers prioritizing performance metrics. Finally, response-ability reveals how trust and accountability are largely delegated to institutional structures, while clinicians report limited legal, organizational, and structural support to respond meaningfully to uncertainty or errors when using AI-CDSS. Conclusions Reanalyzing the same interview material through an abductive STS approach makes sociotechnical dimensions visible that were not the focus of the original analysis. Rather than treating informational requirements as universal or adoption as primarily a matter of technical performance and communication, the findings show how knowledge, value, and responsibility are constituted through situated professional practices and institutional arrangements. Processes and considerations regarding how clinicians make sense of AI-CDSS are not universal but are shaped by social, cultural, and institutional contexts. This analytical perspective underscores the need for context-sensitive, multistakeholder strategies to support meaningful and responsible AI adoption in clinical practice.

items.title: KONSEP AHLIYYAH DALAM HADIS IŻĀ WUSSIDA AL-AMRU ILĀ GAIRI AHLIHI: ANALISIS MA‘ĀNĪ AL-ḤADĪṠ DAN IMPLIKASINYA TERHADAP PENGGUNAAN KECERDASAN BUATAN
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is no longer confined to technical tasks; it is increasingly involved in high-stakes affairs such as leadership, fatwa, and adjudication. Existing studies generally conclude that artificial intelligence lacks ahliyyah and may therefore serve only as a tool, without explaining the eligibility required of the humans who rely on it or capturing its hidden shift from tool to authority. This study aims to formulate a concept of ahliyyah from the hadith Iżā wussida al-amru ilā gairi ahlihi and to contextualize it for the use of artificial intelligence in the amr of qiyādah, iftā’, and qaḍā’. This library research employs the taḥlīlī method of hadith study with a ma‘ānī al-ḥadīṡ approach, comprising criticism of the chain and text, linguistic and rhetorical (balāgah) analysis, examination of the commentaries, and contextualization of the concept of ahliyyat al-adā’. The findings show that the hadith is authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) and that the word wussida, derived from wisādah (cushion), depicts the amr as something leaned upon, so that in the context of artificial intelligence the demand for ahliyyah falls upon the human who leans on it. The study formulates the concept of ahliyyat al-isti‘ānah, the eligibility to seek the assistance of artificial intelligence, resting on competence independence, verification capacity, and ownership of ideas and responsibility. The concept distinguishes three positions of artificial intelligence, namely as wasīlah, as a formal muwassad ilaih, and as a de facto support, and shows that the last is the most subtle form of the death of expertise warned of in the hadith.

items.title: Learning on the record: the observability–authenticity paradox in AI-era STEM assessment
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence tutors produce detailed records of how learners question, reason, and revise, and these interaction traces are increasingly available to teachers and institutions. This commentary examines what happens to the evidential value of interaction traces when they are used to assess learning in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education. I describe an Observability–Authenticity Paradox: the features that make interaction traces informative, such as exploration, expressed uncertainty, and error, are the features that learners have most reason to suppress or manage once they expect the traces to be evaluated. In terms of argument-based validity, such reactivity to evaluation weakens the extrapolation from interaction observed under evaluative conditions to learning activity that takes place without evaluation; it can also reduce the exploration on which learning depends. The threat is greatest when traces generated during learning are used for grading or credentialing without learners knowing when and how, and when inferences rest on behaviors that learners can choose to display or withhold. I distinguish this situation from teachers’ ongoing formative monitoring, consider whether assessment could instead reward productive failure, and explain why differential reactivity is a fairness issue in the measurement sense. I conclude by proposing three design principles (declared, episodic, and learner-owned assessment) and illustrating them with STEM tasks, drawing examples mainly from science education.

items.title: Mapping the Evidence on AI Dependence, Self-Efficacy, and Academic Achievement in Higher Education: A Scoping Review (2015–2025)
items.abstract: Concern has grown that students’ reliance on generative artificial intelligence (AI), and its use for academic dishonesty, may weaken self-efficacy, motivation, and academic achievement, yet evidence on these relationships is scattered across inconsistent labels. Following the Arksey and O’Malley framework and the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR), this review mapped studies published between 2015 and 2025 that examined AI dependence or AI-related academic integrity alongside motivational constructs or academic achievement among higher education students. A Scopus search returned 172 records, of which 21 met the eligibility criteria and were charted. No eligible study predated 2024, eight were set in East Asia and none in Africa, and sixteen were cross-sectional surveys. The apparent inconsistency in the direction of the self-efficacy effect largely disappears once academic self-efficacy, which tended to protect against dependence, is distinguished from AI-specific self-efficacy, which tended to promote it. Dependence was associated with inflated self-efficacy, procrastination, and weaker learning, while associations with achievement were mixed. Amotivation and degree apathy predicted AI-assisted misconduct more strongly than AI use itself. The evidence base remains recent, geographically narrow, reliant on self-report, and almost without longitudinal or intervention research.

items.title: Occupational health and safety standards compliance among construction workers in West Africa: A systematic review of available evidence from Ghana and Nigeria
items.abstract: The construction industry remains one of the most dangerous sectors globally, with West African workers facing particular risks due to labour-intensive methods and limited regulatory enforcement. No previous systematic review has synthesized evidence on compliance with occupational health and safety (OHS) standards among construction workers in West Africa. We searched PubMed, IEEE Xplore, EBSCOhost, Science Direct and Google Scholar for quantitative studies published from June 2001 to August 18, 2026. Studies required extractable data on occupational health and safety compliance outcomes. Quality assessment used the JBI critical appraisal tool for cross-sectional studies. Studies rated as high risk of bias were excluded. Twelve cross-sectional studies met inclusion criteria: seven from Ghana and five from Nigeria. No eligible low- or moderate-risk studies from the other 14 West African countries were identified through this review. PPE use, access and provision varied substantially with helmet use 16.9%, hard-hat use 34.1% and respirator use of 1.7% during relevant tasks. 54.5% respondents in a Nigerian study reported that they did not wear a mask for silica-dust exposure. Welfare facilities were severely neglected, with flushable toilets on only 14.3% of sites. Safety knowledge and training were often more favourable than behavioural measures, but these constructs were not treated as equivalent to compliance. A study found that lack of safety training and inconsistent PPE use were associated with occupational injury, but the causality was not established. Factors associated with poorer compliance included younger age, lower educational level, casual employment, physical barriers and the absence of a construction‑specific regulatory framework. Evidence from Ghana and Nigeria identifies heterogeneous gaps across OHS compliance-related domains, particularly selected PPE practices, organisational implementation and welfare-facility provision. Knowledge, training, PPE availability and PPE use should not be interpreted as interchangeable compliance measures. Standardised multicountry observational studies and evaluations of proposed interventions are needed. Trial registration This systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420250649740).

items.title: Occupational stress among childcare professionals: How psychological safety predicts perceived stress beyond noise, time pressure and physical demands
items.abstract: This study examined how job demands and psychological safety relate to perceived stress among professionals working in early childhood education and care. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources model, the study investigated both the individual and combined effects of workplace demands and explored the role of psychological safety as a psychosocial resource. Specifically, we focused on noise exposure, time pressure, and physical demands, which were selected a priori to capture distinct environmental, temporal, and bodily stressors characteristic of childcare settings. Data were collected through an anonymous survey of 344 childcare professionals employed in daycare centers across Germany. Hierarchical regression analyses were conducted to assess the predictive value of noise exposure, time pressure, physical demands, interaction effects among demands, and psychological safety. The results showed that time pressure and physical demands were significant positive predictors of perceived stress. In addition, the interaction between time pressure and physical demands significantly increased stress levels, indicating a cumulative effect when both demands were high. Noise exposure was not significantly associated with stress in the multivariate model. Psychological safety emerged as a significant negative predictor of stress and explained additional variance beyond the effects of job demands and their interactions. The findings highlight the importance of considering both structural working conditions and team climate in understanding occupational stress in early childhood education and care settings. items.title: Represented Present State Distinguished From Situated State: How Action Can Proceed From an Account of the Present That Does Not Match It
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Represented Present State Distinguished From Situated State, a structural distinction between the conditions that actually hold and a viewpoint’s current representation of those conditions. Either can change while the other remains fixed. Action and projection can therefore proceed from an account that is incomplete or mistaken, while their consequences depend on the situation itself. The account assesses a representation of the present through the evidence and scope supporting its claims. It asks what each instrument, report, inference, or observation establishes, when it was obtained, and which conditions it reaches. No viewpoint requires a complete representation of the situation. The distinction matters where an omitted or mistaken element changes projection, inquiry, or action. A bad outcome alone does not establish a representational error; an accurate account can also be followed by a poor decision or faulty execution. The discussion connects the distinction to Endsley’s account of situation awareness and examines two documented cases. At Three Mile Island in 1979, operators treated a relief valve as closed while it remained open, and their interpretation of the pressurizer level led them to regard the reactor core as covered. On Lubang Island, Hiroo Onoda retained a wartime representation after the war had ended, rejecting contrary reports until his former commander relieved him of duty in 1974. The cases distinguish a mistaken account of an ongoing condition from an account that persists after conditions have changed. Part of the Possibility and Counterfactual Structure series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who constructs a representation, who can challenge it, and who bears the consequences when it diverges from the situation. Its framework can inform human–AI research on state estimation, user modeling, evidence provenance, and whether systems distinguish changes in their internal accounts from changes in the conditions those accounts describe.

items.title: Responsible AI in Public-Serving Institutions: Advances, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Public-serving institutions (government agencies, courts, health systems, social-welfare bodies, and regulators) are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to triage caseloads, allocate resources, detect fraud, and personalize services. Because these institutions exercise coercive and distributive authority over citizens who cannot easily exit the relationship, the stakes of getting AI wrong are qualitatively different from those in commercial settings. This paper surveys the advances, challenges, and future directions of responsible AI in the public sector, synthesizing scholarship on AI in government, algorithmic fairness, transparency, and AI ethics with practitioner-facing governance instruments. We first delimit what makes public-serving institutions distinctive: statutory mandates, due-process obligations, and diffuse accountability. We then map the state of the art across four dimensions (use cases, governance and policy instruments, fairness/transparency/accountability practices, and organizational capacity and procurement) and consolidate representative advances in a described table. We argue that the field has matured from principle proliferation toward operational risk management, exemplified by the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the OECD AI Principles, yet a persistent gap remains between high-level commitments and verifiable practice on the ground. Core challenges include bias and equity harms, threats to legitimacy and due process, opacity and contestability, thin institutional capacity, and fragmented accountability. We conclude with a research and practice agenda emphasizing contestable-by-design systems, sociotechnical evaluation, procurement as governance, participatory oversight, and workforce capability. Responsible AI in public service is less a technical property of models than an institutional achievement sustained over time.

items.title: RiskGuard: a card-based serious game for enhancing education on security patterns and software vulnerabilities in web systems
items.abstract: Abstract Software security education is still insufficiently addressed in many undergraduate computing curricula. Programs often emphasize attack-oriented activities rather than secure design practices, leaving future developers with limited skills to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities. Active learning approaches, such as serious games, offer opportunities to foster engagement and practical understanding of secure development concepts. We aim to design and evaluate RiskGuard , a card-based serious game that supports the teaching of software vulnerabilities and security patterns, investigating its impact on students’ knowledge, intrinsic motivation, and learning experience. We conducted a controlled experiment with 32 undergraduate students from Systems Analysis and Development (SAD) and Information Security (IS) programs. Participants were assigned to either a traditional lecture or a lecture followed by a RiskGuard session. Learning and motivation were assessed using a Knowledge Assessment Questionnaire and the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), complemented by qualitative feedback. Our results indicate that RiskGuard supported concept reinforcement and increased students’ engagement and intrinsic motivation, although it did not outperform lecture-only instruction in immediate knowledge-assessment scores. RiskGuard shows potential as a complementary educational tool for promoting secure software design through game-based learning. This study contributes (i) the design and open resources of RiskGuard , (ii) empirical evidence on its learning and motivational effects, and (iii) insights for integrating serious games into cybersecurity and software engineering education.

items.title: Robots as lab partners: chemists’ perspectives for informing the design of robot-assisted experimentation
items.abstract: Experimental laboratory work involves repetitive, labour-intensive manual procedures and strict safety protocols, making it an attractive area for Robotics and Artificial Intelligence (RAI). With research currently focused on technical innovation, there has been little work investigating the human factors of chemist-robot collaboration, and how these technologies will change the nature of work in chemistry. Understanding chemists’ requirements and perspectives is vital to the successful deployment and acceptance of RAI in laboratories. We examined the potential for robot-assisted chemistry experimentation through the perspective of future users by conducting contextual inquiries and semi-structured interviews with nine experimental chemists at various career levels with and without laboratory automation experience. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to gain a situated understanding of how their work could benefit from automation, as well as their perspectives and opinions on working alongside robots. We found that our participants are open to robot-assisted experimentation and have clear ideas for human-robot partnerships in the lab. We identified eight themes characterising chemists’ desired applications, the implementation requirements, and the perspectives on the adoption of robot-assisted experimentation. These findings show that successful acceptance of robot-assisted experimentation depends not only on technical innovation, but also on addressing the practical barriers and concerns of the chemists who will work alongside these systems. The key concern being that RAI should not constrain, but rather complement the role of the chemist in knowledge discovery. The findings contribute to a set of initial design considerations covering hardware, software, and interaction design for successful integration of RAI in experimental laboratory work.

items.title: Spatial Competition in Fast-Charging Networks
items.abstract: Despite the steady growth of fast-charging networks under government subsidies, the impact of spatial and ownership structures of charging points on pricing strategies of charging point operators (CPOs) and consumer welfare is poorly understood. Given EVs’ limited range, the competition in a fast-charging network is inherently regional. It is unclear whether and under what circumstances CPOs’ competition can lead to regional monopoly, which may hinder the transition to electric mobility. In this paper, we develop a novel framework to examine the competitive dynamics in fast-charging networks that serve regional demand, incorporating delay costs arising from congestion and locational attractiveness of charging stations. At the core of our framework is a spatial competition model, which characterizes the strategic interactions between CPOs and consumers. To overcome tractability issues associated with large networks that arise from real-world settings, we propose a computationally efficient method to optimize CPOs’ pricing decisions. We instantiate the framework in Germany’s Deutschlandnetz, whose awarded regional network comprises 900 charging stations. Using demand projections for 2030, we conduct a series of counterfactual simulations. Our analysis generates four sets of findings. First, price exhibits a strong negative correlation with the local competitiveness level (measured by the density of charging stations), but shows no clear dependence on absolute demand levels. Second, CPOs’ profits are shaped by both local competitiveness and absolute demand. Third, a uniform, stringent price cap may create inefficiencies in network utilization and discourage infrastructure investment, particularly in less lucrative regions. Finally, spatial and ownership constraints in tender rules may fail to ensure competitive outcomes in large-scale charging networks, allowing CPOs to strategically select locations that strengthen their market power ex post. Taken together, these findings suggest that policymakers should enable regionally equitable access to fast charging while ensuring efficient network utilization.

items.title: Teaching Languages in the AI Era: From Innovation to Pedagogical Redesign
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) marks a turning point in language education, accelerating the shift from traditional methodologies toward AI-enhanced learning environments. The aim of this article is to examine the impact of GenAI on language education, understood not as a complementary tool but as a linguistic and epistemological disruption that transforms processes of language production, evaluation, and acquisition. Drawing on a documentary analysis that integrates recent theoretical, empirical, and regulatory sources, the study addresses four interrelated objectives: to reorganize instructional design toward generative tasks of greater cognitive complexity; to identify pedagogical applications of GenAI through tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, NotebookLM, ElevenLabs, Canva, HeyGen, and other emerging GenAI systems; to redefine the teacher’s role as a critical orchestrator and AI-literate professional; and to examine the ethical and linguistic challenges posed by GenAI, including hallucination, discourse homogenization, and risks to academic integrity. The findings indicate that GenAI enhances learning only when embedded within intentional, critically mediated, and well-supervised pedagogy that preserves cognitive engagement, linguistic diversity, and educational equity.[La rápida expansión de la inteligencia artificial generativa (IAGen) marca un punto de inflexión en la enseñanza de lenguas, impulsando la transición desde métodos tradicionales hacia entornos de aprendizaje enriquecidos por IA. El objetivo de este artículo es examinar el impacto de la IAGen en la enseñanza de lenguas, entendida no como una herramienta complementaria, sino como una disrupción lingüística y epistemológica que transforma los procesos de producción, evaluación y adquisición del lenguaje. Mediante un análisis documental que integra fuentes teóricas, empíricas y normativas recientes, el estudio persigue cuatro objetivos específicos: reorganizar el diseño didáctico hacia actividades generativas de mayor complejidad cognitiva; identificar formas de implementación de la IAGen a través de herramientas como ChatGPT, Claude, NotebookLM, ElevenLabs, Canva o HeyGen; redefinir el rol docente como orquestador crítico y profesional con alfabetización en IA; y examinar los desafíos éticos y lingüísticos derivados de la IAGen, como la alucinación, la homogeneización del discurso o los riesgos para la integridad académica. Los resultados del análisis indican que la IAGen solo mejora el aprendizaje cuando se integra en una pedagogía intencional, crítica y supervisada que preserve el compromiso cognitivo, la diversidad lingüística y la equidad educativa].

items.title: The hidden cost of continuity: leadership buffering, boundary erosion, and psychosocial risk in safety-critical systems
items.abstract: Psychosocial hazards can compromise more than worker wellbeing. In safety–critical systems, sustained workload and uncertainty can combine with reduced recovery to weaken the human and organisational capacities through which risks are recognised and controlled. This study develops a systems model of how psychosocial demands, leadership buffering, and boundary disruption can constrain sustained adaptation while operations continue. We examine these dynamics among middle-level leaders in Australia’s mining, oil, and gas sector during the prolonged COVID-19 crisis. Positioned between executive decision-making and frontline operations, these leaders translated changing directives into operating practice while carrying responsibility for continuity and employee wellbeing. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 managers and eight general managers. Team-based thematic analysis was supported by a cross-case descriptive matrix of recurring conditions. Leaders described isolation and disconnection alongside work intensification and fatigue. Persistent uncertainty was often accompanied by anxiety. As organisational arrangements changed, leadership roles expanded and work–nonwork boundaries became more permeable. Middle-level leaders buffered competing organisational and workforce demands, helping operations continue while opportunities for recovery narrowed. Participants described growing difficulty sustaining adaptive effort. The model distinguishes adaptive performance from adaptive sustainability. Continued functioning may coexist with depletion of the resources that enable further adaptation. We extend safety science by conceptualising psychosocial risk as a dynamic organisational process and identifying middle-level leaders as potential sources of safety intelligence. Effective control requires organisations to address how work itself generates exposure, including the staffing and authority available to leaders. Boundary protection and recovery should sit alongside individual support.

items.title: The influence of differentiated instruction on students’ motivation in physical education
items.abstract: Background Physical education (PE) classes are intrinsically heterogeneous, yet students differing in competence, readiness, and motivation are often exposed to uniform instructional demands. Differentiated instruction has been widely advocated as a response to learner diversity, but rigorous evidence regarding its motivational consequences and underlying psychological processes remains limited. Methods We conducted a two-arm cluster-randomized longitudinal trial across 12 secondary schools in Zhengzhou, China. Forty-eight teacher–class clusters comprising 1,152 students aged 12–15 years were randomized to a 12-week differentiated-instruction intervention or usual PE. The intervention systematically adapted task challenge, instructional support, grouping, pacing, progression, and bounded choice to students’ readiness and learning needs. Assessments were completed at baseline (T0), during intervention (T1), post-intervention (T2), and follow-up (T3). The primary outcome was autonomous motivation at T2; secondary outcomes were psychological need satisfaction and frustration, controlled motivation, amotivation, and PE engagement. Three-level longitudinal mixed-effects models and multilevel longitudinal mediation models were used. Results At T2, differentiated instruction produced higher autonomous motivation than usual PE (adjusted difference = 0.49, 95% CI [0.39, 0.59]; standardized effect = 0.72). It also increased psychological need satisfaction (0.53, 95% CI [0.41, 0.65]) and PE engagement (0.46, 95% CI [0.37, 0.55]), while reducing psychological need frustration (−0.46, 95% CI [−0.57, −0.35]) and amotivation (−0.38, 95% CI [−0.47, −0.29]); effects on controlled motivation were small. Longitudinal mediation was consistent with two complementary pathways: greater T1 need satisfaction was associated with higher T2 autonomous motivation (indirect effect β = 0.13, 95% CI [0.09, 0.18]), whereas lower T1 need frustration was associated with lower T2 amotivation (indirect effect β = −0.11, 95% CI [−0.15, −0.07]). Several effects remained evident at T3, although attenuated. Conclusion Differentiated instruction improved motivational functioning in PE by reshaping the instructional conditions through which students experienced challenge, support, progression, and participation. The findings extend differentiated-instruction research beyond pedagogical adaptation by identifying instructional design as a motivationally relevant component of the PE environment and by supporting complementary need-satisfaction and need-frustration pathways linking differentiated instruction with autonomous motivation and amotivation.

items.title: The verification collapse cascade proceeds from rational nonverification through epistemic sedimentation to the dissolution of institutional reality
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence outputs surpass human discriminative capacity, society confronts a novel threat to its capacity to determine truth from falsehood, a threat that requires no intentional attacker. Unlike accounts that locate truth’s erosion in deliberate distortion, the core threat identified here is that truth loses its institutional determinability even where no one is deceiving anyone. This paper proposes the Verification Collapse Cascade (VCC), a three-stage process through which, under the conditions specified here, society’s capacity to determine truth from falsehood degrades along a path that later correction does not retrace. Stage 1, Verification Evaporation, describes rational abandonment of verification when the return on checking AI outputs falls toward zero. Stage 2, Epistemic Sedimentation, describes the accumulation of unverified knowledge through erasure failure and existence fabrication, which the mechanisms that could have prevented it cannot afterwards undo. Stage 3, Institutional Reality Dissolution, describes how fact-determining institutions (scientific, judicial, journalistic, democratic) lose the internal capacity to render fact-fiction distinctions socially binding. The VCC is unified by a phase-transition metaphor reflecting causal dependency: no evaporation, no sedimentation; no sedimentation, no dissolution. Conventional countermeasures presuppose the will to verify and lose efficacy once evaporation advances. The paper proposes that the preservation of human verification capacity and the integrity of the shared knowledge base belong among the primary variables of AI governance, alongside output accuracy.

items.title: Trust and competence calibration in leadership assignment for multi-agent systems
items.abstract: Appropriate reliance on autonomy in multi-agent systems requires operators to continuously evaluate and assign leadership among heterogeneous autonomous agents as task demands and environmental conditions evolve. Research on human-autonomy collaboration has demonstrated promise for anticipated situations and dyadic interactions, but lacks investigation into how operators calibrate trust and competence assessments to support dynamic leadership assignment across multiple agents during unanticipated events. This study investigates temporal modeling of human leadership assignment to multiple autonomous agents based on real-time trust and competence assessment in multi-agent systems. Thirty-nine participants completed three simulated search-and-rescue scenarios involving four autonomous uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs). Each scenario was comprised of twenty object identification trials. Participants rated trust and ranked competence for each UAV in every trial. Results revealed that participants assigned leadership to UAVs based on both competence and trust assessments with respect to the task and environmental conditions. Participants’ assignment performance improved across successive scenarios as they gained experience with UAV capabilities. Network representations of trust, competence and leadership assignment, termed Trust-Competence-Identity-Networks (TCIN), were constructed for every trial and modeled sequentially using Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models (TERGM) to examine the temporal evolution of human perception and leadership assignment (i.e., UAV reliance). TERGM results indicated that trust reflects personalized assessments developed through interaction experience, while competence represents task-specific assessments for leadership assignment. This research extends reliance research on dyadic interactions to multi-agent interactions, introduces the TCIN for studying leadership or reliance dynamics, and provides practical insights for designing adaptive multi-agent systems.

items.title: User Understanding of Robot Learning Evaluations through Task Success Rates and Beyond
items.abstract: Robot Foundation Models (RFMs) and related robot learning techniques represent a promising approach to developing general-purpose home robots. Given the broad capabilities of RFMs, users will inevitably ask an RFM-based robot to perform tasks that the RFM was not trained or evaluated on. In these cases, it is crucial that users understand the risks associated with attempting novel tasks due to the relatively high cost of failure. Furthermore, an informed user who understands an RFM’s capabilities will know what situations and tasks the robot can handle. In this paper, we study how non-experts interpret performance information from RFM and similar robot learning evaluations. These evaluations typically report task success rate (TSR) as the primary performance metric. While TSR is intuitive to experts, it is necessary to validate whether novices also use this information as intended. Toward this end, we conducted a study in which users saw real evaluation data, including TSR, failure case descriptions, and videos from multiple published robot learning projects. The results highlight that non-experts use TSR in a manner consistent with expert expectations and highly value other information types, such as failure cases that are not often reported in RFM evaluations. Furthermore, we find that users want access to both real data from previous evaluations of the RFM and estimates from the robot about how well it will do on a novel task.

items.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
items.abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.

items.title: When Should Humans Intervene? Capacity-Aware Oversight for Financial AI Agents
items.abstract: Human oversight is widely prescribed for high-impact artificial intelligence, but “human in the loop” is not an operational policy when review capacity is finite and agent activity varies over time. We formulate oversight for financial AI agents as a capacity-constrained allocation problem: for each proposed action, a controller decides whether to permit automated execution or consume scarce human review. Unlike a preliminary version of this study, risk scores are not drawn conditional on the realized outcome: observable features are generated first, harm is a hidden logistic function of those features, and a logistic-regression risk model is fit on a separate 60-day, 14,264-action calibration stream, then frozen and evaluated out-of-sample on a held-out 120-day, 28,174-action test stream across five financial domains. The frozen model is well calibrated out of sample (test Brier score 0.091; predicted/observed decile harm rates agree within 1–2 points). We compare no review, random review, a calibration-frozen threshold (uncapped and capacity-truncated), daily risk ranking, a convex risk-severity heuristic, and a genuine expected-loss policy selecting marginal-benefit-maximizing cases under the model’s own optimality argument. The uncapped threshold captures 40.9% of harm value but breaches the 33-action daily capacity on 49 of 120 days; truncating it recovers feasibility at a coverage cost (36.9%). Under the hard constraint, risk ranking captures 38.9% of harm value; the expected-loss policy raises this to 45.5% (a 17% relative gain) and achieves the lowest total expected cost among all evaluated policies, 10.2% below risk ranking at the same 14.1% review rate, while random allocation captures only 13.2%. A 27-cell factorial sensitivity analysis over reviewer effectiveness, review cost, and score discrimination, plus a sweep over harm prevalence and severity dispersion, shows this advantage is stable throughout. Results are computed outputs of the stated synthetic simulation; harm prevention is evaluated in expectation via the assumed reviewer-effectiveness parameter, not observed human-review outcomes. These results show that effective human oversight is jointly a prediction, allocation, and workforce-capacity problem: calibrated risk scores alone are insufficient, and unconstrained cost optimization can redistribute review away from low-severity domains.

items.title: Where Does the Human End? Creative Agency with Generative AI across Five Years of Chinese Digital Painting
items.abstract: As generative AI enters creative work, practitioners must decide where AI assistance ends and human authorship begins. Human-agent interaction (HAI) research has examined AI as a tool, collaborator, consultant, and competitor. The longitudinal problem is how these roles are revised as systems become more capable, public, and economically embedded. We report a five-year interview study with 17 Chinese digital painters, based on annual semi-structured interviews from 2021 to 2025. Participants described recurring but non-uniform patterns of protective resistance, pragmatic task delegation, and, for some, reflective agency repartitioning. Early resistance protected observation, originality, signature, and ownership from AI. Later delegation placed AI in bounded tasks such as references, backgrounds, rough sketches, and client-facing drafts. By 2025, some participants built hybrid workflows around human-only zones, while others described fatigue, precarity, or difficulty locating a remaining human role. Peer norms, emotional climates, and production pressures shaped which delegations felt useful, acceptable, or exhausting. Copyright, authorship, and creative labor remained recurring limits on what participants were willing to delegate. We frame these accounts as longitudinal agency partitioning, the situated work of deciding which stages, responsibilities, values, and claims remain human in creative human-agent interaction. We discuss design implications for revisable agency-boundary controls, provenance scaffolds, and community-facing authorship norms.

items.title: Why do students discontinue learning with ChatGPT? The role of negative information in reducing motivation and learning discontinuation
items.abstract: As conversational AI tools like ChatGPT become increasingly integrated into education, concerns have emerged about how negative information (linguistic cues emphasizing uncertainty, difficulty, or risk) may influence adolescents’ trust and learning behaviors. This study examined associations between negative ChatGPT responses, adolescents’ AI distrust, and learning-related outcomes, including motivation and discontinuation. Among 250 adolescents aged 12–13 who completed a 10-minute ChatGPT-based learning activity on inductive and deductive reasoning, analyses of 195 participants indicated that greater frequency of and initial exposure to negative information were associated with higher AI distrust, which was related to lower learning motivation and greater learning discontinuation. Moreover, dissatisfaction with ChatGPT’s responses moderated these relationships, such that associations between AI distrust and lower learning motivation and greater learning discontinuation were stronger among more dissatisfied adolescents. These findings underscore the importance of how negative AI-generated information is communicated, given its potential implications for adolescents’ trust, motivation, and continued learning engagement.

items.title: AI AS A COGNITIVE ENHANCEMENT TOOL: A FOUR-TIER INSTRUCTIONAL MODEL FOR TEM-8 WRITING
items.abstract: The writing task in Test for English Majors Grade Eight (TEM-8) places high demands on learners’ ability to synthesize information and express critical perspectives. Drawing on teaching practice in the English Writing and Translating Skills Training course for English majors at a Double First-Class agricultural university, this study develops a four-tier model of AI-enhanced writing instruction, with the four tiers corresponding to four ascending levels of cognitive engagement: evaluative regulation, critical analysis, comparative discernment, and selective revision. Using ChatGPT and DeepSeek as supporting tools, the model treats AI as a tool for cognitive enhancement rather than a substitute writer. By analyzing the strengths and weaknesses of AI-generated essays, comparing outputs from different platforms, and using AI critically to revise their own work, students make a cognitive shift from passively receiving feedback to actively directing their use of the technology. This paper explains the rationale, key components, and implementation of the model, offering a replicable framework for integrating AI into writing instruction for English majors in higher education.

items.title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
items.abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

items.title: Algorithmic temporal governance: a sociotechnical theory of labor control, worker adaptation and resistance
items.abstract: Algorithmically mediated work systems are reshaping how organizations govern workers’ time. This paper develops the Temporal Sociotechnical Algorithmic Model (TSAM), a sociological theory explaining how computationally mediated information asymmetries alter workers’ capacity to anticipate, allocate, withhold, and collectively contest their labor time. Drawing on a critical interpretive synthesis of 56 peer-reviewed publications identified through a structured search covering 2000–2024, TSAM begins from a generative condition in which labor time becomes an optimizable organizational resource while workers retain only partial visibility into the processes governing allocation, availability, and evaluation. From this condition, the model specifies three system-level mechanisms: unpredictability, latency compression, and temporal opacity. It distinguishes these mechanisms from temporal anticipatory compliance, an emergent behavioral adaptation through which workers reorganize their availability, responsiveness, and temporal boundaries in anticipation of uncertain consequences. By integrating labor process theory, the sociology of time, and sociotechnical systems theory, TSAM explains how computational mediation reconfigures the informational and temporal conditions through which control is exercised, experienced, and contested. The model further theorizes why resource-protective behavior may become less effective when reduced availability carries uncertain consequences, conceptualizes temporal opacity as epistemic asymmetry rather than simple information deficit, and positions resistance as mechanism-specific modification of algorithmic temporal governance. Five propositions translate these theoretical claims into empirically testable and refutable expectations.

items.title: An exploratory study of total quality management practices and occupational safety and health performance in the mining industry: a plan-do-study-act based framework
items.abstract: The mining industry is dangerous, with all these accidents happening even though safety rules have gotten better over time. It leads to real tragedies, like people dying on the job. This necessitates adopting advanced Total Quality Management (TQM) practices. This study aims to reduce fatalities by implementing a Plan, Do, Study, Act (PDSA) methodology within the organization to enhance occupational health and safety performance. We gathered data from questionnaires handed out to actual miners, focusing on what causes these deadly accidents, and used a tree diagram as a strategic framework for designing safety interventions and identifying learning pathways. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pareto charts to prioritize high-risk activities. The survey findings suggest that management and leadership commitment, safety training and competency, and safety culture were perceived by respondents as the most important factors influencing safety performance, collectively contributing 61.8% of the impact on safety-related activities. After applying a fishbone diagram analysis, human factors and inadequate maintenance schedules were identified as critical root causes. Overall, The study proposes a PDSA approach to improve Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) performance through TQM practices. items.title: Análisis comparativo de la carga mental en el personal administrativo de la Facultad de Ingeniería de la UNACH
items.abstract: Mental workload is one of the main ergonomic risks in today's administrative environments, where psychosocial demands predominate. The objective of this research was to comparatively analyze the mental workload levels of the administrative staff at the Faculty of Engineering of the National University of Chimborazo (UNACH) using the NASA-TLX and SWAT methods, and to determine their relationship with sociodemographic variables. A quantitative, descriptive-correlational, non-experimental, cross-sectional study was conducted with the entire administrative staff (n = 10). Data were processed in SPSS V26 using the chi-square test and Cramér's V coefficient. The results showed a predominance of high mental workload in both instruments (NASA-TLX: 90.0%; SWAT: 60.0%); no statistically significant relationship was found with age or years of experience. These results highlight the importance of implementing psychosocial intervention measures.

items.title: Anthropomorphism and emotional reactions to human–AI collaboration.
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly enters human professional domains , understanding emotional reactions to its involvement becomes critical . We introduce a novel experimental paradigm that distinguishes between AI involvement in “Thinker” and “Doer” roles to examine how the role AI occupies shapes affective and evaluative responses to human–AI collaboration . Across four countries ( N = 1,345), including the United States, the United Kingdom, India, and Colombia, participants evaluated scenarios in which professional jobs were completed under four conditions: human only, full AI automation, human as Thinker with AI as Doer, or AI as Thinker with human as Doer. Our results showed that AI involvement decreased positive affect and appreciation while increasing negative affect . We also found particularly negative emotional reactions to AI executing emotionally charged professions (e.g., artist). Individual differences in AI anthropomorphism consistently moderated these effects. These findings demonstrate that emotional reactions to AI depend on the role it plays and the domain in which it operates. This research highlights the importance of task characteristics and individual differences in understanding human–AI collaboration in professional settings.

items.title: Between legal aspiration and engineering reality: technical and legal barriers to implementing control safeguards for high-risk AI systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in decisions that affect health, safety, welfare and rights, and regulators have responded by requiring “control safeguards”, such as human oversight, robustness and monitoring, for systems classed as high-risk. This article asks why such safeguards are hard to implement and why the difficulty matters for society. It combines doctrinal analysis of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as amended in 2026) with a structured critical review of the technical, human-factors and policy literature. Five technical barriers are identified (model opacity, speed and autonomy, brittle guardrails, limits of human attention and judgement, and the lack of tests for control effectiveness), together with six legal and institutional barriers (open-textured legal standards, uncertain classification, delayed standards and guidance, limited regulatory capacity, fragmented enforcement, and burdens on small organisations). The article argues that these barriers reinforce one another through three gaps: a feasibility gap between what the law demands and what technology can deliver, a verification gap between legal requirements and testable criteria, and a capacity gap between large and small actors and between providers and regulators. Mapping each oversight capability in Article 14(4) to these barriers shows where safeguards are most likely to be formal rather than effective. The article proposes ten recommendations for EU institutions, standard-setters, national authorities, providers and deployers, and considers lessons for lower-capacity jurisdictions, including in Africa, that are drawing on EU-style models. The central conclusion is that regulatory attention should shift from documenting oversight to demonstrating that it works.

items.title: Beyond affective coping and use frequency: academic rumination, generative AI dependency, and two dimensions of perceived cognitive debt
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support learning and emotion regulation, yet frequent or coping-oriented use does not necessarily constitute difficult-to-regulate dependency. It remains unclear how academic rumination and affective coping are positioned relative to dependency and whether dependency is differentially associated with perceived costs to knowledge internalization and independent reasoning. This study examined these distinctions within a single educational psychology model. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 611 current GenAI users recruited through university settings in Tianjin, China (91.7% first-year students). Dependency was a continuous, nonclinical tendency. Ordinal CFA and WLSMV SEM evaluated a prespecified partial association model. Covariate adjustment, four alternative measurement specifications, an AR-score hybrid, and observed-score regressions assessed sensitivity. Results In the reference model, academic rumination was associated with affective coping (β = 0.283), and both were associated with dependency (β = 0.187 and 0.555). Dependency was associated with perceived internalization/memory debt (β = 0.550) and independent-reasoning debt (β = 0.644); their standardized difference was 0.095 (95% Monte Carlo CI [0.032, 0.157]). The corresponding observed-score coefficients were 0.413 and 0.518, with a difference of 0.105 (95% bootstrap CI [0.035, 0.175]). Both serial coefficient products remained positive, but the negative conditional coping-internalization association was not sustained in the observed-score analysis. Reported frequency had no unique association in the combined adjusted model. Alternative measurement models retained robust RMSEA of 0.090–0.097; robust hybrid indices were unavailable. Conclusion The results provide tentative evidence of differentiated self-reported associations among coping, frequency, dependency, and cognitive concerns. Measurement misfit remains unresolved, and the coping-outcome coefficients were sensitive to construct representation. Observed-score consistency for dependency and serial products does not validate the latent structure or establish temporal or causal mediation. These predominantly first-year, Tianjin-based cross-sectional data do not establish objective cognitive decline or generality across student populations.

items.title: Co-creative learning via Metropolis–Hastings interaction between humans and AI
items.abstract: We propose co-creative learning as a novel paradigm where biological and artificial agents (e.g. humans and robots) mutually integrate their partial perceptual information and knowledge to construct shared external representations, a process we interpret as symbol emergence. Unlike traditional AI teaching based on unilateral knowledge transfer, this addresses the challenge of integrating information from inherently different modalities. We empirically test this framework using a Human–AI interaction model based on the Metropolis-Hastings naming game (MHNG), a decentralized Bayesian inference mechanism. In an online experiment, 69 participants played a joint attention naming game (JA-NG) with one of three computer agent types (MH-based, always-accept, or always-reject) under partial observability. Results show that Human–AI pairs improved their categorization accuracy through interaction, and that an MH-based agent converged on a shared sign system aligned with the two agents' joint observations significantly more closely than an agent learning from its own observations alone, a process underpinned by the collaborative minimization of their collective free energy. No statistically significant difference between the MH and Always Accept conditions was detected after Holm correction. Unlike unconditional acceptance under Always Accept, however, the MH-based agent uses an evidence-sensitive acceptance rule based on its local generative model. Furthermore, human acceptance behavior aligned closely with the MH-derived acceptance probability. These findings provide the first empirical evidence for co-creative learning emerging in Human–AI dyads via MHNG-based interaction. This suggests a promising path toward symbiotic AI systems that learn with humans, rather than from them, by dynamically aligning perceptual experiences, opening a new venue for symbiotic and organic AI alignment.

items.title: Construction of the Avatar Trust Scale (ATS): A First Step Toward Measuring Trust in Avatars
items.abstract: Avatars serve as virtual representations of users in digital environments. Their appearance can be freely customized, often leading to discrepancies between visual representation and the user's real identity. Such appearances may unconsciously influence interpersonal trust, complicating the assessment of trustworthiness in virtual interactions. To investigate how avatar characteristics influence trust, we developed and preliminarily validated the Avatar Trust Scale (ATS), a tool designed to quantify trust specifically in the context of avatars. Based on data from a German sample of 840 participants, our findings suggest a two-factor structure: Specific Trust (trustworthiness, security, and willingness to interact) and General Trust (propensity to trust avatars and humans, and avatar literacy). The scale was validated using questionnaire data and behavioral tasks (i.e., trust game, dictator game, ultimatum game). Participants interacted with a virtual agent rather than a user-controlled avatar, providing initial validation in a controlled context and laying the groundwork for future research on avatar-mediated trust.

items.title: Corporate Crisis and Disaster Management in the Digital Era: Building Organisational Resilience through Digital Transformation
items.abstract: Corporate crises are increasingly shaped by interconnected digital infrastructures, global supply chains, cloud services, artificial intelligence and data-intensive business models. This conceptual article examines how digital transformation is changing the character and management of corporate crises. It develops an integrated Digital Crisis Resilience Framework (DCRF). Drawing on crisis management, organisational resilience, dynamic capabilities, stakeholder and socio-technical systems theories, the article conceptualises resilience as a continuous strategic capability rather than a reactive emergency function. The DCRF integrates eight capabilities across the crisis lifecycle. Comparative analysis of the NotPetya/Maersk, SolarWinds, COVID-19, Colonial Pipeline and CrowdStrike cases illuminates the Digital Resilience Paradox: digitalisation can simultaneously strengthen adaptive capacity and increase systemic vulnerability. A five-level Digital Crisis Resilience Maturity Model, research propositions and an implementation roadmap are proposed. The article contributes by integrating fragmented research streams and extending crisis resilience from the firm level to the wider digital ecosystem.

items.title: Decision Time Constraints and Trust Propagation in Multi-Operator Multi-Autonomy Teaming
items.abstract: Modern human–autonomy teams (HATs) often operate under time constraints that limit individuals’ ability to fully evaluate recommendations from the automation and autonomous systems. In these settings, people may rely not only on their own interactions with autonomy, but also on cues from their teammates. This study examines how decision time constraints influence trust propagation in multi-operator, multi-autonomy (MOMA) teams. Participants worked in pairs with two drones in a repeated threat-detection task, making rapid decisions under either standard (3.0 s) or constrained (1.7 s) time conditions. After each round, participants reported their trust in both drones and their teammate, allowing us to quantify how trust propagates based on teammate-reported trust. Results show that trust propagates between teammates in both conditions (p < . 001), with stronger effects under tighter time constraints (3.0 s: b = 0.29; 1.7 s: b = 0.35). These findings highlight the role of social influences on trust in time-constrained environments and inform the design of human–autonomy systems for high-tempo operations.

items.title: Designing Chatbots for Person-Centered Care: Insights from Contraceptive Care in Kenyan Pharmacies
items.abstract: Adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) in sub-Saharan Africa face barriers to contraceptive access and lack decision-support resources tailored to their needs. Many Kenyan AGYW seek contraceptive services in the pharmacy setting, but experience stigma, judgment, and privacy concerns that make it difficult to seek guidance from pharmacists. This work examines how chatbots could integrate into Kenya’s pharmacy setting to support AGYW’s contraceptive decision-making. We presented chatbot prototypes in co-design workshops with AGYW and pharmacy workers to evoke reflections on perceived opportunities, concerns, and preferable futures of chatbot-supported care. Our findings highlight expectations that a chatbot could offer private, non-judgmental spaces for information seeking while shifting trust and authority away from pharmacists, revealing tensions surrounding the distribution of authority, reliance, and control among AGYW, pharmacists, and the chatbot. In response to these tensions, we contribute design guidelines for chatbots to navigate community beliefs and promote shared decision-making by AGYW and pharmacists. More broadly, this work extends research on sensitive health chatbots for youth by showing how such tools embedded within a service delivery setting surface distinct considerations for stakeholder roles and person-centered care.

items.title: Designing Critical Human–AI Learning in Higher Education: The SC-AIM–FAVIC Framework for Analytical and Logical Reasoning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now routine in university study, yet unstructured use risks cognitive offloading, surface learning, and uncritical acceptance of fluent but unreliable output. This article aimed to develop and specify the Symbiotic Critical Human–AI Learning Model (SC-AIM), operationalised through the five-stage FAVIC framework (Formulation, Augmentation, Verification, Integration, Creation), and to set out the assessment instruments and evaluation design that accompany it. Following the Analysis and Design phases of the ADDIE research-and-development approach, we synthesised recent experimental, meta-analytic, and survey evidence to derive design requirements, translated them into a stage-by-stage instructional specification, built a process-sensitive assessment rubric, and defined a quasi-experimental and qualitative validation plan for Indonesian higher education. The results are the model and its components: an evidence-to-design mapping, the FAVIC stage specification, a three-level process-sensitive rubric, and an evaluation design with hypotheses. Conclusion: SC-AIM offers lecturers a concrete, theory-grounded sequence that places human reasoning before and after AI assistance and makes verification an assessed activity, giving higher education a ready-to-use pedagogical model for developing analytical and logical reasoning in the age of generative AI.
